mainTopic: Proving ownership of lost objects with סימנין and witnesses, and how long and in what words a finder must announce his find.
overview: The גמרא first knocks down the idea that we return lost objects by סימנין only because owners are happy with that system, since found loan documents are returned even though the לוה is hurt. רבא then proves from a פסוק that סימנין are דאורייתא. He goes on to rule on competing claims: marks against marks, marks against witnesses, weaving witnesses against losing witnesses, and stronger marks against weaker ones. He applies the same test to a found גט that both husband and wife describe. A new משנה then asks how long a finder must announce: רבי מאיר says until the neighbors know, and רבי יהודה says three רגלים plus seven days. The גמרא explains that 'neighbors' means the neighbors of the place where the item was found. It also asks why רבי יהודה allows only three days of travel when another משנה implies fifteen, and gives three answers. Finally, a ברייתא teaches how the finder numbers the רגלים in his announcement, and the גמרא begins to question that wording.

steps.title: The bundle of documents disproves the 'owners agree' theory
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that סימנין work only because owners agree to them. It points to the משנה that returns found documents by marks, even though the לוה would never agree to that.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about the משנה that says if you find a roll or bundle of documents, you return it? Would you say the borrower is happy to have his loan document given back to the lender?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks an earlier suggestion. That suggestion said we return lost items by סימנין only because owners are happy with that system.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If סימנין worked only because the owner agrees, then everyone involved would have to agree. With a loan document, the לוה is hurt when the מלוה gets it back, so he would never agree. Yet the משנה still says to return it by marks, so the 'owners agree' theory cannot explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is pleasing / acceptable to him

phrases.english: But that which we learned in the משנה:
If one found a roll of documents
or a bundle of documents
he must return it,
would you say so too, that the borrower is happy
to have it returned to the lender?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the previous discussion by attacking the 'owners agree' explanation of סימנין.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that סימנין are only דרבנן and work because owners agree to the system.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Found loan documents are returned by marks, even though the לוה is harmed by that and would never agree.

steps.title: רבא's proof from the פסוק that marks come from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads 'until your brother seeks it' as 'until you examine your brother' to check whether he is a רמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: סימנין are from the Torah. The פסוק says 'it shall be with you until your brother seeks it.' Could you think the finder would give it back before the owner asks for it? So the word must mean: examine him, and see whether he is a swindler or not.
steps.whatsHappening: After the 'owners agree' theory fails, רבא brings a proof from a פסוק that סימנין are דאורייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, 'until your brother seeks it' says something obvious: of course you cannot return an item before the owner asks for it. So רבא reads the word דרש as an instruction to the finder: examine the claimant. The Torah itself wants the finder to check whether the claimant is honest.

keyTerms.meaning: A swindler, someone making a false claim

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Identifying marks are from the Torah,
as it is written:
"And it shall be with you until your brother seeks it"
phrases.notes: דברים 22:2

phrases.english: Would it enter your mind
that he would give it to him before he asks for it?!
Rather, it means: examine him
to see whether he is a swindler
or not a swindler.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the 'owners agree' explanation knocked down, רבא offers a new basis for סימנין: the Torah itself.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 22:2, 'עד דרש אחיך אתו', read as 'examine your brother'.

steps.title: The examining must be done by marks
steps.stepSummary: The examination the פסוק requires must be done with סימנין, so סימנין are דאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this examination done with identifying marks? Learn from it that it is.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his proof. The way to examine a claimant is by asking for marks, so the Torah backs סימנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק tells us to examine, but it does not say how. רבא assumes the examining is done by asking for סימנין, and closes with שמע מינה.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not? (introduces an assumed answer)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, סימנין are דאורייתא, learned from 'עד דרש אחיך אתו', meaning 'examine him to see if he is a רמאי'.

phrases.english: Is it not done with identifying marks?
Learn from it that it is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun in step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: סימנין are a Torah-level way to identify a lost object.

steps.title: רבא opens a new ruling with 'if you want to say'
steps.stepSummary: רבא begins a ruling that depends on סימנין being דאורייתא, but he phrases it as a condition.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If you want to say that identifying marks are from the Torah...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבא starts a new ruling, but the גמרא stops him right away to question his wording. The ruling itself comes in step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'if you want to say' sound unsure, as if רבא is not certain. That sounds odd, since he just proved the point. This is what sets off the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want to say / if you conclude (a conditional opening)

phrases.english: Rava said:
If you want to say
that identifying marks are from the Torah...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the conclusion that סימנין are דאורייתא and begins a practical ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An opening condition: assuming סימנין are דאורייתא. The ruling follows in step 7.

steps.title: Why does רבא sound unsure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא says 'if you want to say' when he already proved that סימנין are דאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If you want to say'?! But רבא already settled for himself that identifying marks are from the Torah!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא interrupts רבא to question his wording. It points out that he does not match what he just proved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא just ended with שמע מינה, a firm conclusion. Opening with a condition right after that seems to take his own proof back. The גמרא wants to know why.

phrases.english: "If you want to say"?!
But he already resolved for himself
that identifying marks are from the Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of step 4 by pointing back to step 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A firm conclusion (שמע מינה) does not fit a later conditional phrasing.

steps.title: His proof can be pushed aside
steps.stepSummary: רבא speaks conditionally because someone could reject his proof, as the גמרא explained earlier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because one could say, as we answered before, that the examining is done some other way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the careful wording. רבא holds that סימנין are דאורייתא, but he knows his proof is not airtight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא suggested that 'examine him' might mean checking him with עדים, not with marks. Since that reading is possible, רבא's proof can be pushed off. So he frames his ruling as 'if'.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא did not change his mind. He still holds סימנין are דאורייתא; he only admits that his proof from the פסוק can be challenged.

phrases.english: Because one could say
as we answered earlier.
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier answer that 'examine him' could mean checking him with witnesses, not marks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording: the proof can be rejected, so a conditional phrasing is appropriate.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's 'if' suggests he doubts that סימנין are דאורייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: He holds they are דאורייתא, but the 'examine him' reading could refer to עדים, so he speaks carefully.

steps.title: רבא's rulings on competing claims
steps.stepSummary: Marks against marks: the finder keeps it. Marks against עדים: it goes to the one with עדים. Marks against marks plus one עד: the single עד counts for nothing, and the finder keeps it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If both claimants give marks, the finder leaves it with himself. If one gives marks and the other brings witnesses, it goes to the one with witnesses. If both give marks and one of them also has one witness, the single witness is treated as if he were not there, and the finder leaves it.
steps.whatsHappening: Now רבא's interrupted ruling continues. He explains how to decide when two people claim the same lost object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Equal marks cancel each other out, so neither claimant gets the item. עדים are stronger proof than סימנין, so עדים win. A single עד is not enough to tip the balance, so it is as if he were not there.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall leave it (the finder keeps holding it)
Is treated as if he is not there

steps.whatToRemember: Marks against marks: the finder keeps it. עדים beat סימנין. A single עד adds nothing when both sides have marks.
steps.whyThisMatters: These rulings set the order of strength between kinds of proof for lost objects: two witnesses are stronger than marks, and one witness does not change the outcome.

phrases.english: Marks against marks: he leaves it with himself.
Marks against witnesses:
it is given to the one with the witnesses.
Marks against marks plus one witness:
the single witness is as if he is not there,
and he leaves it with himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up רבא's ruling that was interrupted after step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Marks against marks: the finder keeps it. Marks against עדים: the one with עדים wins. Marks against marks plus one עד: the עד is ignored, and the finder keeps it.

steps.title: Witnesses to Weaving Against Witnesses to Losing
steps.stepSummary: If one claimant has עדים that the garment was woven for him and the other has עדים that it fell from him, it goes to the one whose עדים saw it fall. The first owner may have sold it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one side has witnesses that it was woven for him, and the other side has witnesses that it fell from him, it is given to the side with witnesses that it fell. We say the first man may have sold it, and then it fell from someone else.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds another ruling to his list. Both claimants have עדים, but the עדים who saw it fall from someone win.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses to the weaving only prove who owned the garment at the start. Witnesses to the losing prove who owned it most recently. Since the first owner could have sold it, the most recent ownership is what counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Witnesses that the garment was woven for this person
Witnesses that the garment fell (was lost) from this person

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the first owner always wins. Owning something once does not mean you still own it, and the later owner wins.

phrases.english: Witnesses of weaving and witnesses of falling:
phrases.notes: One claimant brings witnesses that it was woven for him. The other brings witnesses that it fell from him.

phrases.english: it is given to the one with witnesses of falling,
because we say: he sold it,
and it fell from another person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's list of rulings from Step 7 with a new pairing of proofs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses of losing beat witnesses of weaving, because the woven-for owner may have sold it.

steps.title: Length Measurement Beats Width Measurement
steps.stepSummary: If one claimant gives the length and the other gives the width, it goes to the one who gave the length. Width can be guessed by seeing the owner wear it, but length cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one gives its length and the other gives its width, it is given to the one who gave the length. The width can be estimated when the owner wears the garment and stands, but the length cannot be estimated that way.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא now compares two סימנין. A measurement that an outsider could guess is weaker than one that only the real owner would know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When someone wears a garment, a person looking at him can roughly judge how wide it is. The length is hidden by how it is worn, so knowing it shows real ownership. A סימן counts more when only the owner could know it.

phrases.english: The measure of its length and the measure of its width:
phrases.notes: One claimant knows the length, and the other knows the width.

phrases.english: it is given to the one with the measure of its length,

phrases.aramaic: דְּמִדַּת רׇחְבּוֹ שַׁעוֹרֵי קָא מְשַׁעַר לַהּ
phrases.english: because the measure of its width one can estimate
when its owner wears it and stands,
but the measure of its length cannot be estimated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from עדים to ranking different סימנין against each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Length is a stronger סימן than width, because width can be guessed by looking at the owner.

steps.title: Separate Length and Width Beat a Combined Measure
steps.stepSummary: If one claimant gives the length and the width separately, and the other gives only the combined 'gamma' measure, it goes to the one who gave them separately.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one gives its length and its width, and the other gives its gamma measure, it is given to the one who gave length and width.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא compares a detailed סימן with a less detailed one. Two separate measurements beat one combined number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gamma measure is the length and width added together as one total. Knowing each one separately is more exact than knowing only their sum, so the more exact claimant wins.

keyTerms.meaning: The gamma measure: length and width added together as one number

phrases.aramaic: מִדַּת אׇרְכּוֹ וּמִדַּת רׇחְבּוֹ וּמִדַּת גַּמָּיו –
phrases.english: The measure of its length and the measure of its width, and the measure of its gamma:
phrases.notes: Gamma is the Greek letter shaped like an L. Here it means the length and width counted together as one total.

phrases.english: it is given to the one with the measure of its length and width.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדַּת אׇרְכּוֹ וּמִדַּת רׇחְבּוֹ וּמִדַּת גַּמָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 9's ranking of measurements with a new comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Separate length and width beat a single combined gamma measure.

steps.title: Weight Beats Length and Width
steps.stepSummary: If one claimant gives the length and width and the other gives the weight, it goes to the one who gave the weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one gives its length and its width, and the other gives its weight, it is given to the one who gave its weight.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא ends this series by ranking weight above length and width together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא gives no reason here. Following the reasoning of Step 9, weight is hard to guess just by looking at the garment, so only the real owner is likely to know it. That makes it the strongest סימן in this list.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule behind this list is that a סימן is stronger when an outsider could not easily guess it. Length beats width, separate length and width beat a combined gamma measure, and weight beats length and width together. Witnesses to the most recent ownership beat witnesses to earlier ownership.

phrases.aramaic: מִדַּת אׇרְכּוֹ וּמִדַּת רׇחְבּוֹ וּמִדַּת מִשְׁקְלוֹתָיו –
phrases.english: The measure of its length and the measure of its width, and the measure of its weight:
it is given to the one with the measure of its weight.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדַּת אׇרְכּוֹ וּמִדַּת רׇחְבּוֹ וּמִדַּת מִשְׁקְלוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ranking of measurements that began in Step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Weight is a stronger סימן than length and width together.

steps.title: Husband and wife both give signs of a found גט
steps.stepSummary: A גט is found. The husband and the wife both describe its סימנים, and the ruling is that it is given to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gives the signs of the גט and she gives the signs of the גט, it is given to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The list of competing-סימנים rulings continues with a new case: a found גט that both husband and wife describe. The ruling is that the wife gets it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband claims he never handed her the גט, and the wife claims she already received it. Giving the גט to her means she is treated as divorced. The next step asks what kind of sign makes her description strong enough.

keyTerms.meaning: He says / she says. These are the two competing claimants.

steps.confusionAlert: Here the two claimants are not two strangers fighting over an item. The husband says he never delivered the גט, and the wife says she received it. So 'it is given to her' means she counts as divorced.

phrases.english: He states the identifying marks of the bill of divorce
phrases.notes: The husband is saying he never handed it over, so it's still his.

phrases.english: and she states the identifying marks of the bill of divorce,
phrases.notes: The wife is saying she already received it and dropped it.

phrases.english: it shall be given to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא אוֹמֵר סִימָנֵי הַגֵּט וְהִיא אוֹמֶרֶת סִימָנֵי הַגֵּט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to the series of competing-סימנים rulings, now applied to a גט disputed by husband and wife.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When husband and wife both give סימנים of a found גט, it is given to the wife.

steps.title: Which sign of the גט makes it hers?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which sign the wife gave. Length and width are not enough, because she could have seen them while he held the גט. It must be a hole next to a certain letter.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what signs? If you say by its length and width, maybe she saw it while he was holding it. Rather, she said there is a hole next to such-and-such letter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of sign the wife must have given. It rejects one option and settles on another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Length and width can be seen from a distance while the husband holds the גט. So knowing them does not prove it was ever in her hand. A tiny hole next to a specific letter can only be known by someone who held the גט up close. That is why it proves she received it.

keyTerms.meaning: With what? It asks what exactly is meant.
If you say. It introduces an option that will be rejected.

phrases.english: With what [signs did she describe it]?
If we say with the measure of its length and its width,
perhaps while he was holding it, she saw it.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא – נֶקֶב יֵשׁ בּוֹ בְּצַד אוֹת פְּלוֹנִי.
phrases.english: Rather, [she says] there is a hole in it next to such-and-such letter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what kind of סימן the ruling in step 12 must be talking about.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which סימן did the wife give that is strong enough to win?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not length and width, which she could have seen from afar. It is a hole next to a specific letter, which she could only know by holding the גט.

steps.title: Both give signs of the string around the גט
steps.stepSummary: The husband and wife both describe the string the גט was tied with, and it is given to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gives the signs of the string and she gives the signs of the string, it is given to her.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second גט case. This time the signs are about the string tied around the גט, and again the wife gets it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setup is the same as step 12, but the sign is now about the string, not the גט itself. The next step will explain which detail about the string counts.

keyTerms.meaning: String or thread. Here it is the string the גט was tied with.
It shall be given to her

phrases.english: He states the identifying marks of the string,
and she states the identifying marks of the string,
it shall be given to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא אוֹמֵר סִימָנֵי הַחוּט, וְהִיא אוֹמֶרֶת סִימָנֵי הַחוּט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case to step 12, now about the string tied around the גט.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When both describe the string of the גט, it is given to the wife.

steps.title: Which sign of the string makes it hers?
steps.stepSummary: The color of the string does not prove anything, because she could have seen it while he held the גט. It must be the string's length.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what signs? If you say by white or red, maybe she saw it while he was holding it. Rather, she gave its length.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again asks what sign is meant. It rejects color and settles on the length of the string.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Color can be seen from far away, so knowing it does not show the גט was in her hand. The string is wrapped around the גט, so its full length is only known to someone who held it and unwound it. That proves she received it.

phrases.english: With what [signs did she describe it]?
If we say by [saying it is] white or red,
but perhaps while he was holding it, she saw it?
Rather, [she gave] the measure of its length.
phrases.notes: The string is wound around the גט, so you can't tell its length just by looking at it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same test as step 13, now applied to the string.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which detail about the string proves the wife received the גט?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not the color, which is visible from afar. It is the string's length, which she could only know by handling it.

steps.title: Both say the גט was kept in a case
steps.stepSummary: If both say the גט was in a case, it goes back to the husband. She could know that without ever receiving it, because he keeps all his valuables in that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says it was in a case and she says it was in a case, it is given to him. Why? She knows that everything he has, he keeps in the case.
steps.whatsHappening: In the third גט case both say the גט was kept in a case. This time the husband gets it, and the גמרא gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test from steps 13 and 15 decides this case too. A sign only helps the wife if she could not know it without holding the גט. She knows he keeps everything valuable in his case, so her claim proves nothing, and the גט stays with him.

keyTerms.meaning: A case or pouch for storing things

steps.whatToRemember: A wife's sign proves she received the גט only if she could not have known it just from seeing the גט in her husband's hands or from knowing his habits. A hole by a letter or the string's length works. Size, color, or 'it was in his case' does not.

phrases.english: He says [it was] in a case
and she says [it was] in a case,
it shall be given to him.
What is the reason?
She surely knows
that everything that he has,
he keeps it in the case.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא אוֹמֵר בַּחֲפִיסָה וְהִיא אוֹמֶרֶת בַּחֲפִיסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the other side of the same test: here her sign could come from general knowledge, so the husband wins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If both say the גט was in a case, it is given to the husband, because she knows he keeps all his things there.

steps.title: New משנה: how long must the finder announce?
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says the finder announces until his neighbors know about the item. רבי יהודה says through three רגלים plus seven days after the last one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until when must he announce? Until his neighbors know about it, says רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says three festivals, and seven days after the last festival: three days for the owner to go home, three days to come back, and one day to announce.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It asks how long a finder must keep announcing a found item, and two תנאים disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר gives a short, local measure: enough time for the neighbors to hear. רבי יהודה gives a long, fixed schedule built around the three pilgrimage festivals. He explains the extra seven days: the owner needs time to go home and check that he really lost the item, come back, and announce his loss for one day.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, the משנה text
The three pilgrimage festivals: פסח, שבועות, סוכות

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
And until when is he obligated to announce?
Until his neighbors know about it,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says: three pilgrimage festivals,
and after the last festival, seven days,
so that [the owner] can go to his home, three [days],
and return, three [days],
and announce [his loss] for one day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the סימנים discussion and opens a new topic: how long the duty to announce lasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: announce until the neighbors know. רבי יהודה: three רגלים plus seven days after the last one (3 days home, 3 days back, 1 day to announce).

steps.title: A ברייתא says 'neighbors of the lost item'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that describes the finder's neighbors as 'the neighbors of the lost item.'
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: A תנא taught: until the neighbors of the lost item know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by quoting a ברייתא that words רבי מאיר's rule a little differently. This sets up the next question about what that wording means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said 'until his neighbors know.' The ברייתא says 'neighbors of the lost item,' which is unclear. Whose neighbors are these? The גמרא will ask that next.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא taught: this introduces a ברייתא

phrases.english: גמרא: A תנא taught:
Neighbors of the lost item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes a ברייתא that words רבי מאיר's rule from Step 17 differently.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The announcement must last until the 'neighbors of the lost item' know.

steps.title: Whose neighbors are meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'neighbors of the lost item' means and rejects the idea that it means the owner's neighbors.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are 'neighbors of the lost item'? If you say the neighbors of the owner of the lost item, then if the finder knows who the owner is, let him just go and return it to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא's phrase means. It tests one possible reading and shows it cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the phrase meant the owner's neighbors, the finder would already know who the owner is. Then there would be no need to announce anything. He could simply bring the item back.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say: it introduces a possible reading that is about to be rejected
The owner of the lost item

phrases.english: What are 'neighbors of the lost item'?
If you say: neighbors of the owner of the lost item?
If he knows him,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the finder. If he knows the owner, he knows whose neighbors to go to.

phrases.english: let him go and return it to him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the phrase quoted in Step 18 means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose neighbors does 'neighbors of the lost item' refer to?

steps.title: The neighbors of the place where it was found
steps.stepSummary: The phrase means the neighbors of the place where the lost item was found.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means the neighbors of the place where the lost item was found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct meaning: the finder must announce until the people around the spot where he found the item know about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder does not know the owner. So he announces it near the spot where it turned up, because the owner likely passed through there. That is where people are most likely to know who lost it.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where it was found

phrases.english: Rather, neighbors of the place
where the lost item was found.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא שְׁכֵנֵי מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּמְצֵאת בּוֹ אֲבֵידָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19 with a different reading.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Neighbors of the lost item' means the neighbors of the place where it was found.
steps.whatToRemember: Under רבי מאיר's rule, the finder announces until the neighbors of the place where he found the item know about it.

steps.title: Turning to רבי יהודה's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the start of רבי יהודה's opinion in the משנה to discuss it next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to רבי יהודה's opinion in the משנה. This line only sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה said the finder announces for three רגלים plus seven days. The seven days are three days for the owner to travel home, three days to come back, and one day to announce his loss. The גמרא is about to question the three-day travel time.

keyTerms.meaning: And so on: the rest of the משנה's words are left out

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says: and so on.
phrases.notes: This points back to רבי יהודה's rule in the משנה: three רגלים plus seven days after the last one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves רבי מאיר's view and opens a new discussion about רבי יהודה's view from Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: announce for three רגלים and seven days after the last one.

steps.title: A contradiction: the trip home takes fifteen days
steps.stepSummary: A משנה in תענית says the last pilgrims need fifteen days to get home, not three.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they raised a contradiction: On the third of מרחשון we begin asking for rain. רבן גמליאל says: on the seventh of the month, which is fifteen days after the חג, so that the last person in ארץ ישראל can reach the Euphrates River!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's idea that the trip home takes three days. It quotes a משנה that says some pilgrims need fifteen days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל delays the prayer for rain until fifteen days after סוכות. That way the pilgrims who live farthest away reach the Euphrates before the rain. So the trip home can take fifteen days, which clashes with רבי יהודה's three days.

keyTerms.meaning: And they raised a contradiction between two sources
We begin asking for rain in the עמידה

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about rain itself. The rain משנה is brought only because it shows how long the trip home from ירושלים takes.

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
On the third of מרחשון
we ask for rain.
רבן גמליאל says: on the seventh of it,
which is fifteen days
after the festival,
phrases.notes: 'The festival' is סוכות.

phrases.english: so that the last one in ארץ ישראל can reach
the Euphrates River!
phrases.notes: These are pilgrims who live far away. They should get home before the rains start.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּרְמִינְהוּ: בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה בִּמְרַחְשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the three-day travel time behind רבי יהודה's view in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's assumption that the trip home from ירושלים takes three days
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבן גמליאל's משנה shows that the farthest pilgrims need fifteen days to get home. That contradicts a three-day trip.

steps.title: First מקדש versus second מקדש
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that fifteen days fits the first מקדש period, and three days fits the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: It is not difficult. Here it is talking about the first מקדש, and here about the second מקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף settles the contradiction. He says each source describes a different time in history.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the time of the first מקדש, pilgrims lived far away, so the trip could take fifteen days. In the time of the second מקדש, the pilgrims lived closer, so three days was enough. רבי יהודה's rule fits the second period, and both sources are correct.
steps.whatToRemember: The three-day trip in רבי יהודה's rule and רבן גמליאל's fifteen days do not clash. They describe different periods: the first מקדש and the second מקדש.

phrases.english: רב יוסף said: It is not difficult,
here, in the time of the first מקדש,
phrases.notes: This 'here' is רבן גמליאל's fifteen days.

phrases.english: here, in the time of the second מקדש.
phrases.notes: This 'here' is רבי יהודה's three days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the two sources into different time periods
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Travel time from ירושלים is always the same, so the two sources contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fifteen days was needed in the time of the first מקדש. Three days was enough in the time of the second מקדש.

steps.title: Why population size changes the travel time
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains his answer: in the first מקדש the Jews were very many and spread far, so fifteen days were needed. In the second מקדש there were few Jews, so three days were enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the first מקדש period the Jewish people were huge in number, as the פסוק says they were 'like the sand of the sea,' so we need the full fifteen days. In the second מקדש period they were few, as the פסוק counts only 42,360, so we don't need that much time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the reasoning behind רב יוסף's answer from the last step. It uses two פסוקים to show how many Jews there were in each period.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's logic is that a big population lives spread out over a large area, so the farthest pilgrim has a long way home. A small population lives in a smaller area, so the farthest pilgrim is closer. That is why the first מקדש needs fifteen days and the second needs only three.

phrases.english: During the First Temple period,
when the Jewish people were very numerous,
as it is written about them:
"Judah and Israel were many,
like the sand by the sea in multitude" –
phrases.notes: מלכים א 4:20

phrases.english: we need all this much time.
phrases.notes: He means the full fifteen days from the משנה in תענית.

phrases.english: During the Second Temple period,
when the Jewish people were not very numerous,
as it is written about them:
"The whole congregation together

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע רִבּוֹא אַלְפַּיִם שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שִׁשִּׁים״ –
phrases.english: was forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty" –
phrases.notes: עזרא 2:64. A רִבּוֹא is ten thousand, so four רִבּוֹא is forty thousand.

phrases.english: we do not need all this much time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and supports רב יוסף's answer from step 23 with פסוקים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two sources between two historical periods based on population size.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fifteen days and three days seem to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fifteen days fits the large population of the first מקדש; three days fits the small population of the second.

steps.title: אביי shows the Jews still lived in all their cities
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רב יוסף with a פסוק from עזרא saying all Israel settled in their cities, so the land was still spread out in the second מקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But it is written, 'The כהנים, the לוים, the singers, the gatekeepers, and all Israel lived in their cities.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רב יוסף's reasoning. He quotes a פסוק showing that even in the second מקדש period, Jews lived in all their old cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף assumed a smaller population meant a smaller area to travel. אביי points out that the returning Jews went back to all their cities, so the distance to the far edges of the land was just as long. A smaller number of people does not make the trip shorter.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is רב יוסף, whose answer we just saw.

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
"And the priests and the Levites dwelt, etc.,
and the singers and the gatekeepers,
and all Israel in their cities."
phrases.notes: עזרא 2:70

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that the small second-מקדש population lived in a smaller area and needed less travel time.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק says all Israel lived in their cities, so the land was just as spread out and the distance home was not shorter.

steps.title: אביי flips the two periods around
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues the reverse: in the first מקדש, crowds and caravans traveling day and night made three days enough. In the second, there were no such caravans, so fifteen days were needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since that is so, the opposite makes more sense. In the first מקדש period, when there were many Jews, everyone traveled in groups, and caravans moved day and night, so we don't need that much time: three days are enough. In the second מקדש period, when there were few Jews, no groups, and no caravans moving day and night, we need all that time.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי keeps רב יוסף's idea of splitting the two periods but reverses which period gets which number. He gives a new reason based on how people traveled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the distance was the same in both periods, the real difference is travel speed. With many people, there were always groups and caravans moving day and night, so the trip was fast: three days. With few people, a traveler could only go by day and had no caravan to join, so it took fifteen days.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying the population size does not matter. He agrees it matters, but he says a big population makes the trip faster, not slower.

phrases.english: And since that is so,
the opposite makes sense:
In the First Temple period,
when the Jewish people were very numerous,
and everyone was organized in groups,
and caravans could be found
that traveled both by day and by night –
we do not need all this much time,
and three days are enough.
In the Second Temple period,
when the Jewish people were not very numerous,
and people were not organized in groups,
and caravans could not be found
that traveled both by day and by night –
we need all this much time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on אביי's challenge in step 25 to offer a reversed version of רב יוסף's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources by period, but based on travel speed instead of distance.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יוסף thought the first מקדש needed fifteen days because the land was more spread out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The distance was the same in both periods; the first מקדש had caravans moving day and night, so three days were enough, while the second needed fifteen.

steps.title: The חכמים did not overburden the finder
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the travel time was the same in both periods. רבי יהודה's three days is not the real travel time; the חכמים just did not want to trouble the finder too much.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: There is no difference between the first and second מקדש periods. The חכמים did not burden someone with a lost item more than necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a completely different answer to the contradiction. He drops the idea of splitting between the two periods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבא, the trip home really took fifteen days in both periods, as the משנה in תענית says. But for a lost item, רבי יהודה only gave three days, because asking the finder to wait fifteen days would be too much of a burden. So the two sources measure different things: real travel time versus a fair waiting period for the finder.

keyTerms.meaning: They did not burden / put to trouble

steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to the fifteen-days versus three-days question. רב יוסף says the first מקדש needed fifteen and the second needed three. אביי says the reverse. רבא says the travel time never changed, and three days is simply a limit so the finder is not overburdened.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבא's answer shows that the laws of returning lost items do not ask the finder to go beyond a reasonable effort.

phrases.english: רבא said:
It is no different in the First Temple period
and no different in the Second Temple period;

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הִטְרִיחוּ רַבָּנַן בַּאֲבֵדָה יוֹתֵר מִדַּאי.
phrases.english: the Sages did not burden people with a lost item more than necessary.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אֲמַר: לָא שְׁנָא בְּמִקְדָּשׁ רִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer to the contradiction from step 22, different from both רב יוסף and אביי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the two sources measure different things: real travel time versus a reasonable limit for the finder.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Three days and fifteen days both describe the actual travel time, so they contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The real trip was always fifteen days; רבי יהודה's three days is a limit set so the finder is not overburdened.

steps.title: רבינא proves the finder names the object he found
steps.stepSummary: רבינא learns from the count of days in the משנה that the finder announces the specific item, like 'a cloak,' and not just 'a lost item.' The גמרא agrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Learn from here that when the finder announces, he announces 'a cloak.' If he only announced 'a lost item,' we would need to add one more day so the owner could check all his things at home. Since no day is added, he must announce 'a cloak.' The גמרא agrees: learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא draws a practical lesson from the number of days in the משנה. If the finder only said 'I found something,' the owner would need an extra day to check his belongings, and no such day is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The days counted in the משנה cover only travel and announcing, with no extra day for checking. Someone who hears 'I found a cloak' already knows whether his own cloak is missing, so he needs no checking day. That is why רבינא concludes the announcement names the item.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it. Used to draw a conclusion, or to agree that a conclusion is correct.
A cloak, meaning the specific item
A lost item, with no details

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Learn from this that when he announces,
he announces 'a cloak.'
phrases.notes: A cloak is just an example. He means the finder names the actual object he found.

phrases.english: For if it would enter your mind
that he announces 'a lost item,'
we would need to add one more day for him
to check through his belongings.
Rather, learn from it:
he announces 'a cloak.'
Learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ כִּי מַכְרֵיז, גְּלִימָא מַכְרֵיז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the length of the travel time to a new question: what exactly does the finder say when he announces?
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder announces the specific item he found, as shown by the missing 'checking day' in the count of days.

steps.title: רבא rejects רבינא's proof
steps.stepSummary: רבא says no proof can be brought. Even if the finder only says 'a lost item,' the חכמים did not add an extra day because they did not want to burden the finder too much.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: You can even say he announces 'a lost item.' The missing day proves nothing, because the חכמים did not trouble the finder too much over a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רבינא's proof. He gives another reason why there is no extra checking day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's proof depends on the idea that the days in the משנה must cover everything the owner needs. רבא says that is not so: the חכמים set a limit so the finder is not burdened too much. This is the same idea רבא used in step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say. Introduces the view the other side was trying to rule out.
The חכמים did not put a burden on

phrases.english: Rava said:
You can even say he announces 'a lost item.'
The Sages did not burden
over a lost item more than enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבינא's proof in step 28.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected. רבא does not say the finder must announce 'a lost item'; he says the משנה does not prove either way.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבינא assumed the days in the משנה must cover everything the owner needs. In fact, the חכמים limited the time to spare the finder.
steps.whatToRemember: רבינא: the finder names the item, as the missing checking day shows. רבא: no proof, since the חכמים simply did not want to burden the finder.

steps.title: How the finder numbers the רגלים in his announcement
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that on the first רגל the finder says 'first רגל,' on the second he says 'second רגל,' and on the third he announces with no number.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: On the first רגל he says 'first רגל.' On the second רגל he says 'second רגל.' On the third רגל he just announces, without saying a number.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about the wording the finder uses on each of the three רגלים. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying the number, the finder lets the owner know how much time he still has. The surprise is that on the third רגל he gives no number, and the next steps ask why.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים taught. Introduces a ברייתא.
One of the three pilgrimage festivals

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
On the first festival he says 'the first festival,'
on the second festival he says 'the second festival,'
on the third festival he speaks plainly.
phrases.notes: He announces without saying which number רגל it is.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: רֶגֶל רִאשׁוֹן אוֹמֵר רֶגֶל רִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how the finder words his announcement on each רגל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He names the first and second רגל by number, but announces on the third רגל with no number.

steps.title: Why not say 'third רגל'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the finder does not say 'third רגל,' just as he named the first two.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let him say 'third רגל'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. If he said the number on the first two רגלים, why stop on the third?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern seems broken. Saying 'third' would also tell the owner that this is his last chance, so leaving out the number looks strange.

keyTerms.meaning: And why? Asks for the reason behind a rule.

phrases.english: And why?
Let him say 'the third festival'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the last clause of the ברייתא in step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that on the third רגל he announces with no number.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The finder named the first two רגלים by number, so he should keep the pattern and name the third as well.

steps.title: 'Third' could be confused with 'second'
steps.stepSummary: He does not say 'third' because a listener might mix it up with 'second.'
steps.simpleTranslation: So that people will not come to confuse it with 'second.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'שלישי' (third) and 'שני' (second) sound alike. The owner might mishear and think he still has more time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner heard 'second' by mistake, he would think one more רגל remained and might miss his last chance. On the third רגל no number is said at all, so the owner cannot mistake it for the second.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the finder announces less on the third רגל. He still announces fully. He only leaves out the number.

phrases.english: So that one will not come to confuse it with 'second.'
phrases.notes: The words שלישי and שני sound similar, so the owner might hear 'second' and think he still has time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a practical reason for the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He should say 'third' to keep the pattern of the first two רגלים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He leaves out the number so 'third' is not misheard as 'second.'

steps.title: Then why say 'second' at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to ask: by the same reasoning, the finder should not say 'second' either.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the second רגל too, he should not say the number.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the answer back on itself. If the two words can be confused, saying 'second' could also be misheard. The question finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry about mixing up the two words seems to work in both directions. If the words can be confused, saying 'second' is also risky, so the second רגל should seemingly be announced with no number too.

phrases.english: The second, too
phrases.notes: The question goes on in the next line of the גמרא: he should not say a number on the second רגל either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 32 by using the same reasoning against it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that he says 'second רגל' on the second רגל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the two words can be confused, saying 'second' is also risky, so he should leave out the number on the second רגל too.
